title: She draws. He codes. One month.
author: Most_Industry8958
selftext:
[She draws. He codes. One month.](https://reddit.com/link/1til5bs/video/ou66g3ttja2h1/player)

Working with AI made so much possible. We're almost ready to launch

  


My wife and I just released the official trailer for our first   
Steam game "Return to Lumia" — a 2D mining sandbox launching June 15, 2026.

\*\*How we split AI vs human work:\*\*

I handle all code with Claude (Godot 4 / GDScript). My wife   
shapes the visual direction in Photoshop, working from GPT/DALL-E   
base images and adjusting filters, saturation, and composition   
to fit our pixel art style. Suno for music, ElevenLabs for SFX,   
Meshy AI for character animations (commercial license).

All game design decisions stay human — 10 boss patterns (each unique), 79 quests, 5 NPC story arcs, level design, balance. The AI accelerates generation and implementation; the creative direction is ours.

The biggest surprise for me has been how much the workflow shifts from "writing code" to "specifying intent precisely" — 30% of my time now goes to writing instruction docs for Claude Code, not writing GDScript directly.

Steam page discloses our AI usage transparently. Honest disclosure was non-negotiable.

Steam: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4696030/Return\_to\_Lumia/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4696030/Return_to_Lumia/)

Happy to answer questions about workflow, time allocation, or specific tooling decisions.

comments.author: joeban1
comments.body: That walk animation is rough, whys dudes head flick back so aggresively

replies.author: Most_Industry8958
replies.body: Fair catch. AI image generators can't maintain consistent character frames across animations, so we went with single static sprite + Tween for movement. That head flick is the Tween rotation overshooting on direction change — should've clamped it. Adding to the polish list, thanks.

comments.body: I think it looks pretty damn good.  How was it working with your wife?  I've thought about doing a project with my partner, but...we had enough bad blood with It Takes Two

replies.author: Most_Industry8958
replies.body:
Thanks! It actually works really well because we have a clean split:  
\- I handle all code (Godot 4 / GDScript) and game design  
\- She handles all visual direction and art curation  
\- We collaborate on: tone, narrative beats, NPC personalities, boss design

Zero overlap on daily tasks. The hard part isn't working together — it's not bringing work to dinner.

It Takes Two...yeah, that game's a relationship destroyer.   
We finished it but it was rough. Building together is actually easier than playing together.

replies.author: Most_Industry8958
replies.body:
You're not wrong, those are real limitations.  
The "scaled up" thing is generation at 128px → Nearest Neighbor downscale to 32px. Not how a pixel artist would do it. We chose speed over the proper pixel-art workflow, and it shows.

The cutout edges are something we can clean up before launch — that one's fair to flag.

"Looks like it was done in a month" — yeah, that's literally what it is. Trying to be honest about what we are and aren't.

comments.author: jlb4est
comments.body:
A large thing new devs dont understand with AI generation is the amount of tech debt you accumulate. This project looks rough. The problem is to change these systems and mechanisms to look correct enough for a sellable game will require so much work you may be better off starting from scratch.

The other problem is if I was looking at a resume and saw this as a project it would be a massive negative. This shows me that almost no core aspects of the work is able to be brought to an acceptable level and bringing you on the team is going to be a hellscape of sending your work back for you to fix. If your goal is to land a job in game dev, focus on making some very polished nice assets or mechanics. A couple well done items on your resume are far better than a jumbled mess of a large project.

replies.author: Most_Industry8958
replies.body: I understand that art-related AI technology is lacking. Could you tell me what you consider to be the technical debt?

replies.author: Crimes_Optimal
replies.body:
Dunno what that guy is going to say, but here's another perspective in advance.

Technical Debt is when you take shortcuts early on in development, causing problems down the line from suboptimal code. It's technical "debt" because you're borrowing from the future, taking a shortcut now that you're going to have to pay back later in bug fixes and, most likely, refactoring your code.

Projects like Terraria - which this is a clear clone of - live or die off of continued support and updates. The players expect bugfixes, new content, and continued support. That's how games like Stardew Valley and Minecraft have 10+ year life cycles, by providing a solid foundation of a game and then building on top of that.

AI development severely hampers your ability to build on top of it.

Generative AI is good for getting you something that works, fast, but it isn't going to make you anything that you're going to able to add on to or edit/fix easily. Y'know how chatbots will sometimes say something wrong, and then when confronted, will just correct themselves endlessly until they get to something you'll accept? That happens with code too. You need to be able to read and interpret code in order to take on a project like this.

As soon as you try to start bugfixing or adding content with the AI tools, you're going to start running into major issues. At bare minimum, you need to learn enough about how coding works in order to catch and fix the mistakes, and make it modular in the way you need it to be in order to offer continued support.

replies.author: Most_Industry8958
replies.body:
Thanks for the detailed feedback.

I completely agree with you on this point. That is why, regarding the technical aspects, I do the basic system planning first (for management efficiency) before giving instructions to Claude Code, but it still feels like there are many areas where I am lacking.

replies.author: Crimes_Optimal
replies.body: What do you consider the basic system design? What did you do before feeding it to the bot?

replies.author: Most_Industry8958
replies.body: The systemic designer I envision focused on effective management. As an example, when replacing images in my project, replacing a specific folder automatically updates the combat ports (monsters, variable bodies, NPCs, PCs, etc.). Additionally, when designing related systems, I utilized shared images that could replace the traditional hardcoding of elements other than those for each boat, allowing for wheel transformation substitutes (camera replacement rims, rigidity, gears, etc.).

replies.author: Crimes_Optimal
replies.body:
Okay, so that's all about images and graphical pipelines. None of that has to do with the basic systems - if anything, that's all about polish. It's good to have those things prepared so that you can easily improve them later, but it's not what I'm talking about. 


If you don't have it systems in place to deal with modularity and the need to bugfix and update *at this phase*, it's going to cause you major problems down the line. It sounds like you're relying on the AI to give you the code for almost all of your gameplay systems and everything running in the background. 


That's exactly what's going to cause the problems I'm talking about. 


Management is great. It's good that you have that down. If you don't have a plan in place to deal with problems *in the code*, and the knowledge of coding to let you fix and improve on the generated code, this is as good as your game is ever going to get.

replies.author: Most_Industry8958
replies.body: You're right. What I realized while working this past month is that I shouldn't leave all the coding to AI. For the past two weeks, I've been trying to learn the technical aspects by opening the code and identifying related issues whenever a bug occurs, but it feels like there are limits. I guess I need to do more practice and look up more information. Thanks for the feedback.
